bib.title: SPAE: Semantic Pyramid AutoEncoder for Multimodal Generation with Frozen LLMs

legacy_report:
SOURCE: SPAE: Semantic Pyramid AutoEncoder for Multimodal Generation with Frozen LLMs. Yu, Cheng, Wang, Kumar, Macherey, Huang, Ross, Essa, Bisk, Yang, Murphy, Hauptmann, Jiang (Google, CMU). NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2306.17842v3).
COVERAGE: 69,356 of 69,356 chars; all 27 pages (main text pp.1-10, references, appendix A-D pp.14-26). Only the reference lists were skimmed. Extraction clean. Figures are images; I read only captions, not pixels. No embedded instructions found.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- SPAE turns an image into a pyramid of words from a frozen LLM's vocabulary (top layers semantic, lower layers appearance), so a frozen LLM can read and generate images via in-context learning only.
  number: none
  setup: SPAE trained standalone (no backprop through the LLM); PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5 used as frozen LLMs; 128x128 images, 6 layers.
  quote: "SPAE converts between raw pixels and interpretable lexical tokens (or words) extracted from the LLM's vocabulary."
  where: Abstract, p.1
- Few-shot mini-ImageNet: SPAE beats prior frozen-LLM methods by about 25 points (2-way) and 32 points (5-way) on average.
  number: 2-way average 77.74 (SPAE-PaLM, 2 layers, 5 tokens) and 79.03 (3 layers, 21 tokens) vs LQAE 53.97 and Frozen 51.3; 5-way average 61.86 vs LQAE 29.04.
  setup: Tab.1, 14 settings (task induction, shots, repeats); SPAE-GPT uses GPT-3.5 text-davinci-003 with LQAE's prompt format; SPAE-PaLM uses PaLM 2-L. The authors say GPT and PaLM rows are not for comparing the LLMs.
  quote: "Overall, SPAE PaLM yields +25% and +32% average accuracy improvement over the state-of-the-art on the 2-way and 5-way benchmarks in Tab. 1."
  where: p.6
- Token efficiency: with the same GPT-3.5, SPAE-GPT beats LQAE using 2% of its tokens (5 vs 256).
  number: SPAE-GPT 2-way average 69.51 vs LQAE 53.97; 5-way 53.91 vs 29.04.
  setup: Tab.1, same GPT 3.5 and in-context format.
  quote: "SPAE GPT consistently outperforms LQAE, both using the same GPT 3.5 model and in-context format, while using only 2% of its tokens."
  where: p.6
- More tokens is not better for understanding. Accuracy peaks at layer 3 (21 tokens) and falls beyond.
  number: 2-way average 70.31 (1 token), 77.74 (5), 79.03 (21), 76.76 (85), 71.51 (341), 59.19 (597). 5-way 5-shot-style cells go to "-" at 341/597 tokens because the sequence is too long.
  setup: Tab.5 (appendix), SPAE-PaLM, mini-ImageNet, per-layer.
  quote: "Layer 3 achieves the best overall performance as well as in most of the setups, which balances between the level of details and the burden of the LLM."
  where: p.17-18, Fig.3
- Captioning needs far more tokens than classification. Two layers (5 words) cause hallucinated captions; 4 layers (85 words) give reasonable captions; complex scenes may need all 6 layers (597 words). A baseline tokenizer without semantic guidance or the pyramid makes the LLM hallucinate.
  number: 5, 85, 597 tokens
  setup: COCO captions and COCO-QA, 10 in-context examples; VQA is 10-way 1-shot; qualitative (Fig.5), not quantified.
  quote: "Reasonable captions start to appear with 4 layers or 85 words, while complex scenes may still need the full 6 layers of 597 words."
  where: p.8
- VQA: SPAE beats Frozen without backprop through the LLM.
  number: Real-Fast-VQA 14.3/15.9/15.1 (1/3/5 inner shots) vs Frozen 7.8/10.1/10.5.
  setup: Tab.3, SPAE-PaLM, few-shot.
  quote: "Unlike Frozen, SPAE training does not require backpropagation through the LLM."
  where: p.7
- Reconstruction: with 597 tokens (6 layers), SPAE matches or beats a 256-token VQGAN. With fewer tokens it is worse.
  number: 128x128 ImageNet FID 4.41 (SPAE, 6 layers, 597 tokens) vs 5.48 (VQGAN, 256 tokens); at 5 layers (341 tokens) FID 9.49. Video FVD 6.35 vs 6.79. 256x256 FID 3.60 vs 4.04. ImageNet-21k variant FID 3.08.
  setup: Tab.2; ImageNet val; Kinetics-600 for video.
  quote: "While SPAE may have more lossy reconstruction compared to VQGAN when using a similar number of tokens, this is compensated by going into deeper layers."
  where: p.6-7
- Ablations (5-way 1-shot accuracy and recon). A frozen codebook alone ruins semantics. Semantic loss lifts accuracy sharply. Removing the perceptual loss wrecks reconstruction.
  number: baseline VQ 19.6%; +frozen codebook 19.5% (FID 7.44); +semantic loss 46.2% (FID 5.17); 2-layer RQ FID 11.94/6.05 vs SAQ 12.30/5.08; no perceptual loss FID 40.47 (IS 33.41) but 69.5% accuracy at layer 3.
  setup: Tab.4, mini-ImageNet 5-way 1-shot.
  quote: "The perceptual loss leverages a trained network with access to classification labels, but removing it results in a surprising improvement in classification accuracy while greatly hurting the reconstruction."
  where: p.9-10
- Generation with a frozen LLM works only in a narrow regime. Direct generation was shown on 32x32 MNIST: 50 context samples, each digit is 37 tokens in 4 layers. The LLM answers queries like "an image of 1+7" with an 8. Beyond 32x32, the authors switch to in-context denoising. Single-step decoding (stride infinity) fails; progressive decoding works. VQGAN and LQAE tokenizers fail under the same procedure.
  number: 8k context fits "less than a dozen 128x128 images"; 10 example pairs, corruption 50% down to 20% (rates 0.5 to 0.23 in 0.03 steps); PAR for layers 1-5, PNAR for layer 6.
  setup: PaLM 2 frozen, qualitative results only (no FID or human eval for generation).
  quote: "For higher resolutions, the context length restricts the number of examples. For instance, a context window of 8k tokens can only hold less than a dozen 128 ×128 images."
  where: p.5, 8-9, App. B.3
- Design: Streaming Average Quantization (SAQ) replaces residual quantization (RQ), because RQ's residual scales and summed word embeddings fit a frozen codebook badly. The pyramid concentrates semantics in few tokens.
  number: 6 layers of 2^k x 2^k tokens, k=[0,1,2,3,4,4], giving 1, 5, 21, 85, 341, 597 cumulative tokens. A non-pyramid layer needs at least hw (256) tokens.
  setup: SPAE 59M params (image), 176M (video); CLIP ViT-L/14 as semantic scorer; semantic loss on the first 5 layers with thresholds 0.98/0.95/0.9/0.85/0.8.
  quote: "RQ [22, 47] is applicable but yields worse results in this context, as revealed by our ablation studies."
  where: p.4
- Appearance moves to deeper layers when more layers are added. SPAE-8 (8 layers, 1109 tokens) reaches FID 3.89; its CLIP score at layer 1 is 0.2051 vs 0.1879 for the 6-layer model.
  number: FID 4.78 at 853 tokens, 3.89 at 1109.
  setup: Tab.6, appendix.
  quote: "With more token layers, the model gains larger capacity for both semantic and appearance, where the appearance gets pushed into deeper layers."
  where: p.18-19
- Training cost and efficiency. Within 40% of the training steps SPAE has better FID than the final VQGAN checkpoint.
  number: image SPAE: batch 256, 450k steps. Video SPAE: batch 512, 130k steps, 5.8k TPUv4-hours.
  setup: ImageNet ILSVRC2012 (image); Kinetics-600, 384k videos (video).
  quote: "within 40% of the training steps, SPAE shows better FID than the final VQGAN checkpoint."
  where: p.6, 19
- Leakage check. Excluding the 20 mini-ImageNet classes from tokenizer training gives only a slight drop (2-way, 2 layers: 77.74 down to 72.93; 3 layers: 79.03 down to 74.98).
  number: 72.93, 74.98
  setup: SPAE-disjoint (Tab.5). The tokenizer is trained on ImageNet train, which may overlap mini-ImageNet. The LLMs may also have seen those classes.
  quote: "As expected, we observe a slight decrease in performance, since both SPAE and LLMs need to generalize to the test classes that are outside the training data distribution."
  where: p.18
- Multilingual tokens appear, because the vocabulary is multilingual. Examples: koffie (Dutch), kaffe (Danish) for coffee. Some tokens are odd or have inappropriate connotations.
  number: none
  setup: qualitative (Fig.4).
  quote: "We have found that the generated tokens occasionally include slang terms or words that create inappropriate connotations related to the subject depicted in the image or video."
  where: p.7, 10

LIMITS
- Authors: "More tokens are required to achieve the same level of reconstruction when using the frozen language codebook... The capability of in-context learning is significantly constrained by the acceptable sequence length... the resolution, quality, and diversity is far from the recent text-to-image models" (p.10).
- Generation results are qualitative only. There is no FID or human evaluation for LLM-generated images.
- Few-shot comparisons are against Frozen and LQAE, which are 2021-2023 baselines. Frontier VLMs trained on image-text pairs have since far surpassed this on understanding, so the "surpassing state-of-the-art" claim is dated. It holds only under the frozen-LLM, in-context setting.
- The authors say the method is "more effective when backpropagating through LLMs by prompt or adapter tuning", which they did not test. Models used are PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5 text-davinci-003.
- Only 4 samples fit for image-to-video, which limits quality (Fig. 20).
- Possible train/test overlap, partly addressed by SPAE-disjoint.

BUILDS ON: VQ-VAE (van den Oord 2017); VQGAN (Esser 2021); LQAE (Liu, Yan, Abbeel 2023; frozen BERT word-embedding codebook); RQ-VAE (Lee 2022); Frozen (Tsimpoukelli 2021); FROMAGe (Koh 2023); CLIP (Radford 2021) as the semantic scorer; MAGVIT 3D-VQGAN (Yu 2023, ref [45]) for the appearance loss and video; MaskGIT (Chang 2022) for the cosine corruption schedule; in-context learning (Brown 2020).

CODE: no code. Prompt templates worth keeping (App. B.2, p.15-17):
- Classification (PaLM 2): `Answer with "lion" or "vase".\n<SPAE string from a lion image>\nThis is a lion\n...<query>\nThis is a`
- Captioning: `Generate a caption sentence based on words describing an image.\nQ: <SPAE string from image 1>\nA: <Caption for image 1>...`
- Generation (PAR): `Learn a new language and predict the 4 tokens following the examples.\nC:<condition>\nQ:<SPAE string (token 1-12)>\nA:<SPAE string (token 13-16)>`
- Decoding settings: greedy decoding, max 20 tokens for captions, 4 for VQA and classification. Generation samples 8 candidates, retries at temperature T_i = ψ·Σ2^j with ψ=0.01 if all are shorter than the stride.
- Core equation (3): the quantized embedding at layer l is the average of the token embeddings seen so far (streaming average).

FIGURES
- Fig.1 (p.2): framework. The pyramid of layers (4, 5 and 6 layers = 85, 341, 597 tokens) with a frozen LLM codebook and CLIP semantic loss. Best single overview.
- Fig.3 (p.6): accuracy vs number of layers, peaking at layer 3. Shows that more tokens hurt understanding.
- Fig.4 (p.7) and Fig.13 (p.21): token pyramid examples (espresso machine: presso, blender, Thermo, stove; multilingual koffie/kaffe). Makes "words as image tokens" concrete.
- Fig.5 (p.8): captions by layer L1-L6 vs baseline (L1 hallucinates; L5-L6 correct).
- Fig.6 (p.8): MNIST queries such as "1+7" answered with a digit image.
- Fig.7 (p.9): decoding strides, infinity stride fails.
- Fig.9 (p.9): SPAE vs VQGAN vs LQAE on denoising.
- Fig.11 (p.14): RQ vs SAQ geometry.
- Fig.14 (p.22): coarse-to-fine reconstruction, layers 5 to 8.
- Fig.2 (p.5): in-context denoising prompt layout.

PROBLEMS: Equations and table layouts are partly garbled in the extraction (Eq.1, Tab.2 and Tab.4 column alignment). I took the numbers from rows that were unambiguous. The Tab.4 "SPAE 2-layer" row mixes the FID of layers 1 and 2. The text references "Tab. 3" for ablations in the appendix, but it is Tab. 4. In Tab.1 the "Avg" and "Task induction" headers are scrambled; per-column mapping was inferred from Tab.5's layout. No prompt-injection text found.
